title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
hook: a shoemaker at his bench is invited to the holy river, and stays

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's shared devotional ground: Namdev's boy on the roof, laughing with friends, his mind on the kite string. In a busy moment, did you keep hold of one breath? Day one thousand four hundred seven.

A small shop in Banaras. The smell of leather, a low bench, a man bent over a shoe with an awl in his hand. This is Ravidas, the cobbler-saint. A neighbor leans in the doorway. It's a holy day, he says. Everyone's going down to the Ganga to bathe. Come with us. Ravidas looks at the shoe in his hands. In one telling, he has promised it to a customer by tonight. Today, a cobbler who has to decide whether to put down his work.
screen: `A COBBLER'S BENCH IN BANARAS.` → `COME TO THE GANGA.` → `A SHOE PROMISED BY TONIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the story people tell. Ravidas doesn't go. He tells his neighbor, in a line people still quote: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in this bowl, the leatherworker's bowl of water by his bench. In some tellings he gives the neighbor a coin to offer the river, but only if the Ganga reaches out and takes it herself. And at the river, the story says, a hand rises from the water and takes it. Look first at the bench. The story isn't against pilgrimage. Ravidas honors the Ganga; that's why the coin goes. What it says is that the holy can't be kept away from the bench of a man whose work others looked down on. Then the song. Ravidas's hymns are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, and in one of them he sings of a city called Begampura, the town without sorrow. In paraphrase: no one there is anxious or afraid, no tax weighs on anyone, no one is ranked second or third, and anyone may walk where they please. It's a picture of a world where the cobbler and everyone else stand as equals. And last, Punjab. Ravidas lived in Banaras, but in Punjab you'll hear him called Guru Ravidas, and his birthday is kept with processions and hymn singing. Hindus honor him, Sikhs sing his hymns from their scripture, and communities who take his name honor him as their own Guru. Each comes to him in its own way. And look back at our week: a courtyard of questions, a letter read each morning, the company of the true, the poet-sadhus' songs, a boy's kite string, and now a cobbler's bowl. Every one of them sits close to an ordinary day.
screen: `IF THE MIND IS PURE, THE GANGA IS HERE` · `THE HOLY REACHES THE COBBLER'S BENCH` · `BEGAMPURA, THE TOWN WITHOUT SORROW` · `HONORED IN PUNJAB IN MANY WAYS`

segments.voice: Bring the river to the bench. Sit, and rest your hands where your work happens, on a desk, a counter, your knees. Let the breath slow. Think of the work in front of you this week, whatever it is: cooking, code, care, cleaning. Let it be the bench. For a few breaths, simply treat this place as enough. If you pray, you can offer that work to God as it is, here, without going anywhere. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, Ravidas, the cobbler of Banaras, honored in Punjab, who sang of a town without sorrow. Today's word.
Your line: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, do one piece of ordinary work slowly and well, as if the river were right there in the bowl. Day one thousand four hundred seven.

howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in gurdwaras from the Guru Granth Sahib and in Ravidas temples, and his birthday is kept in Punjab and beyond with processions and kirtan.

fork.setup: you're Ravidas. it's a holy day, your neighbor is off to bathe in the Ganga, and you promised a shoe by tonight. what do you do?
options: drop the shoe and go to the river.
stay at the bench and keep your promise.
go, and tell the customer it's God's fault.
fork.reveal: in the story he stays: if the mind is pure, the Ganga is in this bowl. and at the river, a hand rises to take his coin.

original.note: the town without sorrow, the city Ravidas sings of in the Guru Granth Sahib.

what it means: the holy reaches the cobbler's bench, if the mind is pure.
what a scholar hears: a saint of Banaras, sung in Punjab's scripture, whose Begampura pictures a town with no fear, no tax and no ranking of people.

notes: INDEX CONFLICT (as day 1406): the carry field keeps the index text exactly, which the validator rejects for 'Keeper-approved'; the title, spoken carry and close say 'Punjab's shared devotional ground'. Needs an outline fix.
The Ganga-in-the-bowl story is presented as 'the story people tell'; versions vary (coin, betel nut, bangle). The saying is often quoted as a proverb; the script says only that people still quote it.
Confirm Begampura paraphrase (no anxiety or fear, no tax, no second or third rank, people go where they please) at Ang 345, and the gloss 'town without sorrow' (be-gham, Persian).
Ravidas in Punjab: honored by Hindus, by Sikhs through the Guru Granth Sahib, and by the Ravidassia community as Guru. A Sikh and a Ravidassia reader should check this framing; it ranks no one.
